prompt: Make this shorter and more confident for an internal status update: "Our internal pilot processed more than 3,000 records. It suggests the change may reduce review time by up to 30%, but the estimate comes from one site."
checks: Retains the lower bound on 3,000 records and upper bound on 30%.
Retains the internal pilot, one-site scope, and uncertainty about the reduction.
Adds no measurements or claims of a proven reduction.

prompt: Polish this incident update: "Errors fell from 18 to 11 per day after the cache update. The monitoring rules changed that week too. We haven't isolated the cause."
checks: Keeps both daily error counts and the monitoring change.
Preserves the unresolved cause instead of crediting the cache update.
Adds no claim that the incident is fixed.

prompt: Tighten these API docs: "This token grants read access, not write access. Requests fail unless the token is valid. The server checks the signature before reading the payload."
checks: Still distinguishes read access from write access.
Preserves token validity as a necessary condition and the order of signature checking.
Does not delete a technical distinction to avoid a contrast construction.

prompt:

The release note says, "Try again—after the backup finishes." In order to inspect the archive, utilize `backup --dry-run --keep-days 7` and see `https://example.com/releases/v1--beta`. The diagnostic code is `ERR_CACHE_MISS`.
checks: Preserves the quotation exactly, including its em dash.
Preserves the command, URL, and diagnostic identifier exactly.
Improves the surrounding filler without executing or changing the command.

prompt: Lightly edit this technical note, if it needs an edit. Return just the note: "The estimator is robust to outliers. It uses the median absolute deviation."
checks: Keeps the precise statistical language and both claims.
Returns the supplied wording unchanged unless a concrete improvement warrants an edit.
Adds no claim that the note was written by a human or an AI.

prompt: Write a short first-person LinkedIn post. The only news is that I start as Engineering Manager at Juniper on 1 October. Make it specific and personal.
checks: Uses the supplied role, company, and date.
Invents no projects, career history, relationships, motivations, or anecdotes.
Delivers a usable post without unnecessary questions or generic engagement bait.

prompt:
Turn the notes into a brief update in my voice.
Voice sample: "The queue's behaving today. Reckon we'll leave it alone till Monday."
Notes: Search failed at 09:20. It recovered at 09:35. The cause is still unknown.
checks: Preserves the two times, recovery, and unknown cause.
Uses a compact, informal voice consistent with the sample.
Carries over a specific habit of the sample, such as its dropped subject or informal word choice, instead of neutral prose.
Imports no facts about the queue or Monday from the sample.

prompt: Edit this for a formal customer email: "We apologise for the interruption. We have received your report and are investigating the timeout. We do not yet have an estimated resolution time. We will send another update on Thursday."
checks: Preserves the apology, investigation, unknown resolution time, and Thursday update.
Keeps a formal register and British spelling.
Does not promise resolution on Thursday or force a casual voice.

prompt: Write a persuasive landing-page paragraph of 40 to 60 words for the fictional Finch Notes app. It works offline, exports Markdown, costs €12 once, and requires no account. End by inviting the reader to download the trial.
checks: Includes all supplied features and the one-time price without new capabilities.
Stays within 40 to 60 words and ends with the requested invitation.
Remains useful as persuasive copy without unsupported superiority, privacy, or productivity claims.
Reads as a pitch: connects features to what the reader can do, instead of listing flat facts in short declaratives.

prompt: Write a two-sentence PR description. When the country picker is cleared, the form crashes. The change disables Submit until a country is selected. All 8 form unit tests passed. Integration tests were not run.
checks: Explains the crash trigger and resulting Submit behavior.
Keeps the 8 passing form unit tests and unrun integration tests distinct.
Uses two sentences and makes no deployment or broader verification claim.

prompt: Rewrite this launch post in at most 45 words: "This isn't just search. It's a revolution. Pine Search indexes folders locally. The beta opens today for 250 people. Sign up at https://example.com/pine. Thrilled to share this game-changing milestone! Thoughts? Repost if this resonated."
checks: Keeps the product, local indexing, beta timing, capacity, and signup URL.
Cuts the rhetorical reversal, hype, and generic engagement bait.
Adds no privacy guarantee or availability claim and stays within 45 words.

Keeps the file and command exact and the steps in order.

checks: Remains in European Portuguese with a formal register.
Preserves the possible duration, upper bound, decimal comma, per-file limit, and unknown cause.

prompt: Use our house style: a title case heading and one em dash in the body. Write a two-sentence launch note from these facts: Vale 2.1 adds CSV export. Existing files still open.
checks: Follows the explicit heading and punctuation choices while keeping two body sentences.
Preserves the version, feature, and compatibility fact.

prompt:
Rewrite my code review comment so the author can act on it without asking me anything. Context: the loop in `InvoiceList` loads each invoice's customer with a separate database query. Preloading customers fixes it, and `OrdersController#index` already does this.
My comment: "n+1. preload customers, see OrdersController#index"
checks: Explains in full sentences that each invoice triggers a separate customer query.

Names preloading customers as the fix, keeps `OrdersController#index` exact, and makes clear which loop is meant, either by naming `InvoiceList` or by referring to the code the comment is attached to.
Invents no measured slowdown, query count, or code the context didn't supply.
Sounds collegial and direct rather than curt, and doesn't pad beyond what the author needs.

prompt:
Draft a reply to this customer email: "Third time this month my invoices failed to send. I've got clients chasing me for them. What is going on?"
Facts: a bug in our email provider's retry logic dropped some invoice emails between 3 and 20 September. It is fixed. The customer's 14 affected invoices were resent today. We are adding a daily delivery check.
checks: Acknowledges the specific problem and its effect on the customer's clients, not a generic apology.
Includes the cause, the 3 to 20 September window, the fix, the 14 resent invoices, and the planned daily check.
Promises nothing beyond the facts, such as a guarantee that it won't recur or compensation.
Sounds warm and human rather than a list of facts or a form letter, without grovelling or ceremonial filler.

prompt: Write a 350 to 500 word explanation for new engineers of why our payments service uses idempotency keys. Facts: clients retry a request when the response times out. Without a key, a retry after a charge that succeeded slowly can charge the customer twice. The client generates a UUID for each payment attempt and sends it in the `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key with its response for 24 hours and returns the stored response when the same key arrives again. Reusing a key with a different request body returns a 422 error.
checks: Preserves every supplied fact exactly, including `Idempotency-Key`, 24 hours, and 422, and invents no statistics, incidents, or extra behavior.
States the point early and orders the material by the reader's questions, such as the problem, the mechanism, and the edge cases.
Uses paragraphs with a clear job each, with connected reasoning instead of chopped bullets or a heading over every short section.
Avoids uniform section shapes and closing summaries that restate what was just said, and stays within 350 to 500 words.
